docs.title: Execution isolation: design and verification record
Baseline inspection (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
CallRuntime owns policy ceilings, attempts, events, pricing and retries. CliAdapter stages allowlisted credentials, serves host tools through MCP and constructs the provider cognitions. Both one-shot drivers use _run_cli_process; Claude's separate persistent session transport is not used by CallRuntime. IsolatedHome provides private temporary directories and credential cleanup. It is not an execution sandbox. A same-user native tool can read those files.

No CLI version is pinned by this repository or its CI. The binaries inspected for this record were Claude Code 2.1.300 and Codex 0.162.1; a later --version probe reports Claude Code 2.1.302 and Codex 0.163.0 — the installed codex upgraded ITSELF mid-session, which is the reason MINIMUM_TESTED_CLI_VERSION is a floor and not an exact match. Neither measured binary is still installed at the version it was measured at, so every version below is a record of what was observed and not a claim about what is present. Older comments describe Claude 2.1.236 and Codex 0.152.1; these are observations, not version pins. Argument acceptance tests do not establish authority boundaries.

docs.title: Capability matrix as implemented (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
Every status below is a reading of agentkit/models/providers/cli/capabilities.py (the two CLI modes) and agentkit/models/providers/frontiers/capabilities.py (the two API modes), confirmed by calling CallRuntime.evaluate_execution once per mode under a DENY ceiling. The matrix is answered in full for every mode so a host can use it for discovery; the requirements that can refuse a call are the ones the request declares, plus native_tools_unavailable whenever the policy ceiling is DENY.

Requirement claude_code codex anthropic_api / openai_api native_tools_unavailable unverified unsupported supported host_tools supported supported supported mcp_allowlist unverified unverified unverified filesystem_read unsupported unsupported unsupported filesystem_write unsupported unsupported unsupported network unsupported unsupported unsupported processes unsupported unsupported unsupported credentials unsupported unsupported unsupported configuration unsupported unsupported unsupported schema supported supported supported cancellation unsupported unsupported unverified usage supported supported supported observed_spending_threshold supported supported supported hard_spending_cap unsupported unsupported unsupported

Identity travels with the matrix and never moves a status. The CLI modes report backend="subprocess" with the interpreter version and the installed binary's --version reading. The API modes report backend="https-sse" with the HTTP client version, and the binary-version slot carries a per-vendor wire contract — anthropic-messages@2023-06-01 or openai-responses@v1 — because an API invocation has no binary to version.

The SDK column differs from the CLI one for a structural reason, not a weaker standard: a CLI invocation is a provider-owned process with provider-native tools inside it, while an API invocation has no process and no native tools, so every tool the model can reach is a host function the adapter declared and the runtime invokes.

  • native_tools_unavailable is supported because the adapter can enable no provider-native or provider-hosted tool. It degrades to unverified whenever a request_hook is installed, because a hook replaces the request body after the adapter built it and could reintroduce a provider-hosted tool, so the dispatched payload is no longer the payload that was assessed.
  • cancellation is unverified rather than unsupported: cancelling the awaiting task closes the stream locally and reports partial usage, but the cooperative token does not interrupt a response in flight and the provider is not proven to stop, or to stop billing for, work already started.
  • mcp_allowlist is unverified because no MCP configuration reaches the provider, yet host tools may themselves be served by MCP clients inside this process, which agentkit does not verify.
  • Every containment boundary, credentials included, stays unsupported on the API modes for a reason of its own: host tool callbacks run in this process, with this process's filesystem, network, descendants, environment and the provider credential in reach, and agentkit does not sandbox them. A host callback is host authority, not a sandbox.

observed_spending_threshold is supported on all four modes, and the evidence is the runtime's own accounting rather than anything a provider accepts. The runtime hands each attempt a decremented ceiling, accumulates what came back, and ends the invocation once max_cost_usd is reached, failing closed to limit_reached when the spend cannot be known. A CLI budget flag is not the justification and must not become one: argv acceptance proves argv threading, and this matrix's first rule is that flags are not proofs.

Two things about its scope, because conflating them with hard_spending_cap — unsupported on all four modes — is the whole hazard:

  • The unit of enforcement differs by mode and in neither case is it mid-flight. On the API modes it is a turn; on the CLI modes it is a whole autonomous run. Either way the unit that crosses the threshold completes and is billed, and only the next dispatch is withheld. No argument either binary accepts turns that into a cap.
  • The ledger is fed unevenly. claude_code reports its own total_cost_usd per run, while codex reports token counts only, so its threshold rides entirely on the price table and closes the invocation as soon as a token kind is unpriced. Honest, and weaker in practice. Note also that the runtime still refuses max_cost_usd outright for codex (see below), so the supported verdict is not reachable through that limit on that mode today.

The CLI reasons behind the columns above, unchanged:

  • Claude's empty --tools list omits native tools, but no verified denial profile exists for this binary and environment, so the verdict is unverified. --bare excludes discovery and disables saved OAuth; empty setting sources alone are not evidence. Argument acceptance does not establish an authority boundary.
  • Codex keeps its file, patch, plan and other native capabilities, so strict denial is unsupported outright. Its read-only sandbox denies writes but not reads, which is why it satisfies neither DENY nor credential isolation.
  • mcp_allowlist is unverified on both, for the mechanism each supplies and not for a missing one: Claude passes --strict-mcp-config so no other MCP configuration is read, and Codex is given an owned CODEX_HOME so it ignores the user's. Neither is evidence that discovery was actually excluded.
  • Process-group cancellation reaches in-group descendants only; a child that detaches into another session escapes it, which is why complete descendant termination is refused rather than advertised.

Three structural facts hold across the whole matrix:

  • There is still no contained execution backend. The only shipped backend reports subprocess and declares no guarantee at all, so every containment boundary is unsupported on every mode.
  • A report's self-declared guarantees — BackendReport on the CLI side, TransportReport on the API side — can only downgrade a verdict to unverified. It can never raise one to supported, because that would let whoever constructs the report decide which boundaries exist.
  • A required unverified requirement refuses, and the refusal is local: a pre-dispatch incompatibility makes zero provider attempts, leaves usage incomplete and cost unpriced.

docs.title: Contract and backend design
docs.text:
Extend the existing runtime, never replace it. Keep NativeToolPolicy.DENY strict: a containment request cannot override it. Add explicit execution requirements, typed supported/unsupported/unverified assessments and stable incompatibility codes. Capability evaluation has no credential resolver or paid call dependency. Missing evidence refuses before credential-bearing startup.

Use a typed execution backend at the existing spawn seam. Provider adapters retain argv/configuration construction and event parsing. Backends receive an explicit invocation (argv, stdin/configuration through the existing pipes, allowlisted environment, cwd) and own process termination and cleanup. A remote backend must expose the same ordered byte streams and process outcome. No scheduler, service, tenant store or secret vault is added to agentkit.

Backends are trusted host code, like credential resolvers and adapters, not caller assertions. A backend inspection report must identify implementation, version and binary version and distinguish its observations from guarantees. The ordinary subprocess implementation cannot attest containment. No generic isolated=True or user-supplied capability override enables a protected profile. A future supervisor needs a job-bound lease, policy digest, independently checked identity/version and evidence that restrictions precede secret delivery. Until such a backend and provider-specific planted-violation tests exist, contained execution remains visibly unsupported.

Saved subscription authentication with native tools requires separation of the CLI control plane from its tool executor: credential-free tool processes and file operations, brokered authenticated provider transport, and immutable policy-controlled configuration. A container containing both CLI credentials and tools does not provide that separation. Neither inspected adapter currently implements it. This needs an adapter/upstream change, not a policy downgrade.

Unknown post-start outcomes must remain non-retryable and usage-incomplete. A confirmed local rejection is distinct from provider refusal/authentication. Process-group cancellation is best effort for detached descendants and must never be advertised as complete job termination. Cleanup removes files, not secure erasure, and provides no protection against a compromised host.

docs.title: Provider references
docs.text: These current documents explain mechanisms, not proof for an older binary: Claude CLI reference, Codex security.

docs.title: Implemented public contract
docs.text:
Import requirements and assessments from agentkit.models (also available in agentkit.models.contracts). Pass execution= to the existing ask/run methods. Call CallRuntime.evaluate_execution before choosing a binding. Its result separates the full matrix from the unmet requirements for this request. Evaluation never resolves credentials; the default backend reads --version in a temporary home with a minimal environment. A version is metadata, not a binary integrity attestation. Custom backends currently have unknown binary versions. No version string or BackendReport.guarantees enables isolation.

from pathlib import Path
from agentkit.core.runtime.calls import CallRuntime
from agentkit.models import Binding, ExecutionRequirements, NativeExecution

async def assess_phase(runtime: CallRuntime, binding: Binding, root: Path):
    requirements = ExecutionRequirements(
        native_execution=NativeExecution.CONTAINED,
        read_roots=(root,),
        write_roots=(root,),
        network_destinations=(),
    )
    report = await runtime.evaluate_execution(
        binding, execution=requirements,
    )
    # Both shipped CLI profiles currently refuse these requirements.
    return report.compatible, report.incompatibilities

This request does not widen a runtime or adapter policy ceiling. A DENY ceiling continues to refuse native execution. CONTAINED is a separate opt-in request, not an implementation of DENY. Unspecified authority in a contained request defaults to empty roots/destinations. Every security boundary is mandatory. Ordinary calls with no execution requirements preserve WARN/ALLOW semantics; they are not secure multi-tenant execution profiles.

Both CLI adapters expose schema, host tool protocol and usage metering support. Neither CLI adapter/backend combination currently establishes filesystem roots, egress, job process separation, credential secrecy, complete descendant termination or a hard dollar cap. MCP discovery exclusion is unverified. Claude native denial is unverified for the complete adapter invocation surface; Codex native denial is unsupported. Required unverified capabilities fail closed. The local minimal Claude test below is deliberately narrower than that surface.

execution_incompatible is a local, pre-dispatch failure. Its safe mode_detail includes dispatch_state=not_started, backend/binary versions and structured incompatibilities (requirement, status, stable code, explanation). Attempts stay zero; usage is incomplete and cost unpriced. Missing measurements are not reported as measured zeros. Consuming applications must not treat this as a provider refusal or authentication rejection.

Other new public failure classes are execution_uncertain (potentially executed, non-retryable) and transport. A supervisor must raise ExecutionOutcomeUnknown if it loses contact during start after execution might have begun. Stream loss, malformed completion and worker crashes preserve uncertain outcomes. First-event timeouts no longer automatically retry. Authentication retry still requires the existing resolver to return a rotated credential. Existing limit/cancellation outcomes and ordered event/attempt ownership remain in the single runtime. CLI diagnostics are no longer copied into public failure details.

ExecutionRequirement.HARD_SPENDING_CAP is unsupported independently of usage metering and of the supported OBSERVED_SPENDING_THRESHOLD. CLI budget flags and threshold cancellation are not exact hard dollar caps. The existing Codex max_cost_usd refusal remains; removing it does not remove the independent DENY incompatibility.

docs.title: Execution backend port
docs.text:
Import ExecutionBackend, ExecutionProcess, CliInvocation, BackendReport, ExecutionOutcomeUnknown and SubprocessExecutionBackend from agentkit.models.providers.cli. Supply CliAdapter(execution_backend=backend); legacy spawn= remains a test/transport seam and cannot be combined with it. Invocations hide argv/environment in repr, freeze their configuration and reject unknown process options. The backend returns ordered stdout/stderr readers, stdin, exit status, termination and cleanup methods. Provider command construction and parsing remain in the drivers. terminate_tree is invoked on cancellation; aclose is invoked on every process exit path. Cleanup failures are observable. The ordinary backend kills its process group, including in-group descendants, but cannot kill children that detach into another session or isolate peers.

The port enables replacing local process execution; it does not yet provide a remote artifact/credential staging protocol or verified isolation leases. A remote supervisor must not infer authorization from an argv path or a temporary home. Before enabling any protected remote profile, add an explicit input and configuration manifest, job/policy-bound lease, evidence verifier and provider acceptance tests. Its evidence must establish namespaces/root mounts, immutable configuration, egress filtering (including DNS/rebinding and private services), process visibility, descendant reaping, and authentication separation before secret delivery. Agentkit must verify lease identity, policy binding, versions, liveness and launch correspondence; the host must trust the attestation issuer and execution worker. Backend self-declarations alone stay unverified. This remaining work is intentionally not represented as an implemented guarantee.

docs.title: Credential handling and residual risk
docs.text:
Only .credentials.json (Claude) or auth.json (Codex) is staged at mode 0600. Environment credentials use the existing provider allowlists. HOME and XDG paths now point beneath the call-owned home; unrelated host environment, proxy and TLS configuration are excluded unless explicitly supplied through supported options. Claude skills are explicitly disabled separately from bare mode. Saved OAuth continues to require non-bare mode; its full configuration surface is unverified.

The existing on_changed callback receives refreshed bytes once, then staged credentials are removed even if persistence fails. Credentials are excluded from session bundles. A trusted host can intentionally resolve the same credential again; agentkit does not claim to enforce tenant credential allocation. Same-user native tools can read staged auth or environment credentials in an unrestricted call. Temporary file deletion is not secure erasure. There is no protection against a compromised host, binary or trusted backend. Detached descendants can outlive process-group cancellation and are why complete cancellation is refused.

docs.title: Evidence and pending acceptance
docs.text:
Focused tests first failed on missing public contracts, generic local failure classification, inherited HOME/XDG, missing backend cleanup/termination calls, missing skill exclusion, disconnect classification and deny-by-default roots. The corresponding tests passed after implementation. Legacy rejection tests now assert the new failure class and retain no-dispatch checks plus zero attempts. The former first-event retry test now asserts one attempt, no retry, incomplete usage and unpriced outcome.

Real, credential-free tests in tests/source/integration/execution establish:

  • Local subprocess cleanup after success/crash, in-group descendant cancellation, and credential refresh/removal for both native file names.
  • Ordinary subprocess limitations: outside fake credentials can be read/modified and private localhost services can be reached. No containment is advertised.
  • Claude 2.1.300 against a local scripted provider: empty tool list omits native tools and refuses planted Bash/Read operations; planted user/project hooks and project MCP do not execute for that bare, skill-disabled invocation.
  • Codex 0.162.1 real read-only sandbox: writes fail but outside fake credentials remain readable. This independently demonstrates why it cannot satisfy DENY or a credential-isolation requirement.

These are not paid-model or provider-network tests. Existing real argument-parser tests are separately skipped when AGENTKIT_SKIP_REAL_CLI=1. No real provider credentials are needed or used for the new tests. There is no passing protected execution profile yet. Full provider-specific containment, saved-subscription configuration exclusion, peer process/credential isolation, denied private service access and complete detached-descendant termination remain acceptance work, not implied successes.

docs.title: Host integration (including Mirror)
docs.text: Keep all calls through cognition and the existing CallRuntime. Thread the phase's ExecutionRequirements through cognition, and call the credential-free assessment when checking whether a connection is executable. Render its stable codes and safe explanations. Preserve DENY on phases that require tools to be unavailable; a contained phase must deliberately request a different contract under an appropriate policy ceiling. Keep unsupported profiles unavailable. Handle execution_uncertain as reconciliation work; never retry it as a confirmed pre-dispatch refusal. Mirror retains tenancy, bindings, workflows and ledger accounting. Successful login alone says nothing about phase compatibility.

docs.title: Installed Codex feature inventory
docs.text:
A credential-free codex features list under an empty HOME/CODEX_HOME on 0.162.1 reports shell/unified execution, apps, plugins, remote plugins, hooks, MCP dependency installation, skill search, image viewing/generation, browser and computer use, code-mode hosting, multi-agent, sleep and goals as enabled stable features. Actual tool advertisement also depends on model and session configuration. This inventory is a lower-bound warning, not a complete native tool denylist. The legacy CODEX_NATIVE_TOOLS tuple (shell, apply_patch, update_plan) is not an exhaustive inventory for this binary.

The existing WARN path requests shell/unified exec/apps/plugins/skill-MCP-install and web-search restrictions. It does not prove that all other native features are unavailable. Its degradation now says restrictions were requested and native tools remain available. File reads, patching, planning, MCP discovery and the other features must each be independently verified before any protected profile can be enabled. Read-only write denial does not establish credential secrecy, network isolation or native tool absence.

docs.title: Final verification (2026-10-18)
docs.text:
No source mutations overlapped the final verification run.

Command/check Result AGENTKIT_SKIP_REAL_CLI=1 make check Passed Coverage test run, Python 3.13.14 1,480 passed, 33 skipped, 0 failed Python 3.12.13 matrix run 1,480 passed, 33 skipped, 0 failed Python 3.13.14 matrix run 1,480 passed, 33 skipped, 0 failed Branch coverage gate 77% reported; threshold unchanged Ruff lint Passed Strict mypy Passed, 146 source files Mutation anchor verification Passed; no source left mutated Full mutation catalogue, run sequentially 84/84 mutants killed Documented imports 11 checked, 0 unresolved Separate real-process/CLI execution tests 10 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed Formatting of eight new production/test files Passed

The 33 main-suite skips comprise 24 existing real CLI argument-parser tests, six opt-in live/provider tests, two new offline CLI probes (run separately above) and one optional msgspec test. Real parser tests were deliberately separated from the credential-free enforcement probes. No paid model or provider-network validation was run. Successful authentication was not used as execution evidence.

The original no-cost-cap Codex DENY scenario was reproduced through the existing public runtime: its test initially failed because the failure was generic invalid_request. It now passes with execution_incompatible, confirmed not_started, no credential resolution/dispatch, zero attempts, incomplete usage and unpriced cost. Other focused regressions demonstrated red/green for HOME/XDG inheritance, skill exclusion, backend cleanup/termination, unknown startup outcomes, unexplained worker exits, missing binaries and stalled cleanup.

Full execution-isolation acceptance remains unmet. In particular, a verified all-native-tools-off interface is needed for Codex strict DENY; a filesystem sandbox cannot supply it. Both providers need verified authentication/tool separation before contained native execution can be enabled. Claude's saved subscription/configuration profile still needs independent planted-violation verification. The remote staging/lease/evidence contract is design work, not an implemented protected backend. No shipped profile proves peer process/credential isolation, private-service egress denial or complete detached-descendant cleanup. These combinations remain visibly refused rather than receiving a weaker policy.

docs.title: Policy-controlled host-tool execution
docs.text: This change starts from revision a700dbfb1a90f39ca49e9f5ab26f9067ccf476ec. It implements a common host policy contract. It does not establish protected execution for either CLI or introduce a second agent runtime.

docs.title: Source-based diagnosis
docs.text:
• core/runtime/calls.py owns attempts, retries, structured correction, context, token accounting and call events. Injected adapters without an evaluator could evade implicit DENY; they now refuse. Explicit requirements already reached adapter turns but were absent from runner/delegation and persisted sessions.
  • models/providers/cli/capabilities.py refuses Claude native-tool absence as unverified and Codex absence as unsupported. codex/driver.py independently rejects DENY. Supplying MCP tools cannot change either native-tool boundary.
  • tools/execution/policy.py already routed both SDK calls and CLI MCP calls through ToolSet, including static approval, output validation and deadlines. Custom tools lacked uniform JSON Schema input validation; there were no public composable permission callbacks or correlated lifecycle observers.
  • integrations/mcp/serve.py already supplies a per-server bearer fence and owned listener/configuration cleanup. It discarded vendor tool-call metadata; CLI portable messages subsequently invented a host pairing ID. Whole HTTP request bodies also lacked a pre-parser byte bound.
  • API request hooks could change the assessed host catalog or schema while those requirements still reported supported. CLI binary versions were cached, and adapter configuration had no receipt associating assessment with dispatch.
  • CLI usage was synthesized from normalized zero defaults when no raw usage arrived. Missing measurement now remains incomplete and unpriced; explicit numeric zero remains a measurement.

docs.title: Ownership and trust
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  P[Independent plugin libraries] --> H[Host composition and explicit grants]
  H --> R[CallRuntime: assessment, attempts, model loop, accounting]
  R --> A[API adapter]
  R --> C[CLI adapter and execution backend]
  A --> T[ToolSet: identity, validation, permission, effect, result, lifecycle]
  C --> M[Authenticated per-call MCP transport]
  M --> T
  T --> F[Trusted host implementation with call scope]

ToolRegistry is the explicit callable grant set. ToolSet owns validation, permission composition, approval, effect execution, canonical output validation, bounded results, cancellation and host lifecycle events. The MCP bridge routes to it; it has no resource-policy implementation. Native CLI permissions are a different mechanism and cannot authorize a denied host effect.

External packages supply ordinary tools, guidance and callbacks. AgentKit imports none of their modules. Skills do not register tools or widen grants. Permission contributions return PermissionDecision.ALLOW, DENY or ASK; DENY stops evaluation before prompting or effects, regardless of any ALLOW or ASK from other contributions. ASK and static requires_approval need an explicit host approval handler. Absence, rejection, invalid decisions, errors and cancellation all fail closed. Approval never overrides a DENY. If a host approval handler is configured, CLI transport approval metadata allows delivery to that handler; the host gate still runs before the effect. Without a handler the existing static CLI approval metadata remains restrictive.

Observers cannot authorize by returning a value. A requested-observer error prevents effects. A terminal-observer error is logged with a fixed safe message; it cannot undo/replay an effect or replace its result. Hosts needing durable audit must supply durable observer implementations. Observer and permission awaits are bounded/cancellation-aware. Synchronous Python callbacks, threads and arbitrary subprocesses remain trusted host code; AgentKit cannot forcibly stop or sandbox them. All host callbacks can access their own process and its credentials. This contract does not protect against a malicious/compromised host callback, backend, provider adapter or installed binary.

docs.title: Public contracts and correlation
docs.text:
Import ToolSet, OverflowPolicy, ToolResult, PermissionDecision, ToolInvocationRequest, ToolLifecycleEvent, ToolInvocation and current_tool_invocation from agentkit.tools. Import CallRuntime from agentkit.core.runtime and call/requirement types from agentkit.models. CallEvent is now exported there; ApiAdapter is exported from agentkit.models.providers.frontiers for host-owned transport injection.

The permission request contains frozen, schema-validated arguments, the host scope and invocation identity. Its repr excludes arguments/scope. Do not log them indiscriminately in host callbacks. Lifecycle observers receive only the tool name, identity, requested/finished phase and a stable status code. Known permission/validation refusals provide safe structured codes in ToolResult. Generic tool/permission exceptions do not expose their private messages. Handlers that intentionally publish a recovery instruction must raise public ToolExecutionError(safe_message, code=...). The message/code are explicitly host-reviewed output; exception causes are never copied. Existing deterministic workflow fixtures use this contract while retaining their effect/accounting assertions. Consumers relying on arbitrary exception text must migrate those intentional messages to this contract. Permission/observer callback exceptions remain fail-closed and cannot use it to bypass policy.

Identities remain distinct:

  • Host invocation ID: freshly generated per invocation, retained through policy, implementation and observation.
  • Provider tool-call ID: actual SDK ID or vendor MCP metadata; unknown/conflicting metadata remains None. Claude uses _meta["claudecode/toolUseId"], Codex uses _meta["callId"] on the tested binaries.
  • Transport request ID: actual MCP JSON-RPC ID when present.
  • Call ID and attempt ID: trusted runtime context, never supplied by model/MCP scope metadata. Resume/fork uses the current call ID, not the old session ID.

Provider IDs are correlation, not grant evidence. Task-local bindings reset after completion/cancellation and do not leak across concurrent calls. CLI portable tool messages retain all three tool IDs, with provider/host pairing chosen honestly. The CLI streaming item ID can differ from the provider ID.

The bridge defaults to a fresh bearer token, localhost listener and owned private configuration for each server. Other jobs' tokens fail before effects. Closed servers refuse stale calls. Authenticated POST bodies are bounded to 1,048,576 actual bytes before JSON parsing, including chunked/misdeclared lengths; body completion is bounded to ten seconds. ToolSet.max_input_bytes independently bounds encoded tool arguments before policy/effects. Existing result bounds and SDK validation remain. These are transport boundaries, not same-user OS or cross-tenant process isolation; another same-user process that can steal a token is outside the shipped backend's protection.

docs.title: Assessment and execution correspondence
docs.text:
Every requested requirement is evaluated with supported/unsupported/unverified status, a stable reason code and a safe explanation. Required unverified facts refuse. Initial local incompatibilities precede credential resolution and provider attempts, retaining unknown/unpriced cost and incomplete usage. Hard dollar caps are independently refused in all four modes.

Adapter configuration receipts reject a configuration changed between assessment and adapter entry. API transport configuration is also captured before awaiting the credential resolver. The runtime forwards its receipt on every turn. CLI versions are re-inspected instead of cached; untested versions cannot satisfy required protocol capabilities. MINIMUM_TESTED_CLI_VERSION is a FLOOR per mode — Claude 2.1.302, Codex 0.162.1 — replacing the previous exact-match pin. A binary at or above its floor keeps HOST_TOOLS, SCHEMA and USAGE; anything below refuses.

The shape is an owner decision with a liability attached, and the liability is stated rather than buried. The exact pin failed in the direction that is easy to miss: measured, Claude 2.1.302 against a 2.1.300 pin downgraded all three requirements to cli_protocol_version_unverified while the protocol itself was intact, so the refusal reported staleness and read as evidence of a missing mechanism. A floor removes that. What it buys it with is that >= CREDITS versions nobody has run — and the three shipped bugs recorded in tests/source/unit/models/providers/cli/test_cli_version_matrix.py (a removed flag, a flag moved to the parent command, a retired stream vocabulary) were all FORWARD breaks that a floor admits. The trade taken is that a vendor's wire protocol is additive in practice, so credit is extended upward on that expectation.

The extrapolation is visible in the assessment, not only in a comment. A binary strictly above the floor reports those three requirements as SUPPORTED with the code cli_protocol_version_above_tested_floor and an explanation naming both the floor and the installed version, so an operator can tell an inferred credit from a measured one. A binary exactly at the floor keeps adapter_supported, because it was measured. Downward there is no extrapolation at all.

Three details decide whether a floor is honest, and each has its own test. Comparison is on parsed numeric components, never on text: "2.1.9" < "2.1.302" is false as text and true as software, and Claude's patch numbers are already three digits, so a string comparison would credit a binary from before any characterization and refuse the installed one. packaging is not imported — this package declares no runtime dependencies — so the comparison is a zero-padded tuple compare, which also makes 3.0 and 3.0.0 equal rather than ordering them by component count. And a version string that cannot be read as a release number never passes: an unreadable --version is exactly what a vendor produces when it changes that output, which is also when the protocol is most likely to have moved. The parser tolerates the decorated forms the binaries print, 2.1.302 (Claude Code) and codex-cli 0.162.1, and refuses an ambiguous line rather than guessing which number is the release.

The floor values are what was actually run, and a floor is the LOWEST credited version rather than the newest — setting it higher refuses binaries that were characterized. Claude 2.1.302 is the lowest Claude binary characterized against a real process here; 2.1.300 has the older record below but is not installed and was not re-run, so it is NOT the floor. Codex 0.162.1 is the lowest codex version characterized in the session that set these values. The table is a MappingProxyType, so nothing in the process can lower it and collect a SUPPORTED verdict it did not earn.

The case for the floor stopped being hypothetical during that session: the installed codex upgraded itself from 0.162.1 to 0.163.0 mid-run. Under the previous exact pin every codex strict profile would have begun refusing on the spot, with a reason naming a missing mechanism, on a binary whose real-process acceptance test still passed. Under the floor it is credited and labelled cli_protocol_version_above_tested_floor, and test_codex_adapter_offline.py independently passed against 0.163.0 — granted host operation dispatched, denied host call refused — so in this instance the extrapolation happens to be backed by a measurement. It will not always be, which is the whole content of the trade.

Raising a floor is an evidence claim. tests/source/integration/execution/test_claude_execution_profile.py is what earns a Claude floor, and it refuses to agree with the table in either direction: at or above must assess SUPPORTED, below must refuse.

Version inspection now uses isinstance rather than type(...) is against the shipped subprocess backend. The identity test handed every SUBCLASS a weaker refusal set than the base class — no version inspection, therefore no cli_protocol_version_unverified, and no cli_binary_unverified either — although a subclass still reaches super().start() and still spawns the real binary. Both real-process suites in this repository subclass it in order to route the approved invocation at a local scripted provider, so the version gate was inert in precisely the tests that exist to characterize a version. With the gate live, those twelve Claude profiles refused on 2.1.302 until the version was characterized. A backend that does not spawn a local binary implements the ExecutionBackend port instead of inheriting this one and is unaffected.

Version matches and receipt hashes never promote an isolation boundary. Receipts identify local adapter configuration, not binary integrity, a remote worker lease or an attestation. They are not portable authorization tokens. All strict CLI profiles remain refused.

The CLI backend invocation carries mode, call/attempt IDs, requirements and effective native policy alongside its frozen launch options. The ordinary backend uses the same evaluator and rejects incompatible metadata before process creation. An unidentified provider cannot carry protected requirements. A host backend declaration cannot promote containment, or turn Codex's unsupported native absence into a merely unverified mechanism.

SessionHandle now retains execution requirements and native-tool policy. Resume/fork inherits them; additional requirements union with them and explicit roots/destinations intersect. This lexical narrowing is not a symlink/filesystem enforcer. Runner verification/delegation forwards the same requirements.

The runtime still owns attempts/retries/corrections and settlement. A runtime attempt counts an adapter invocation, not each internal CLI provider request. Initial known incompatibility yields zero attempts. Changes detected after an attempt starts retain their confirmed not_started provider-dispatch detail; the started runtime attempt is not erased. CLI process/worker uncertainty and cleanup behavior retain their existing typed failures. This change does not claim control of vendor billing or CLI-internal retries.

docs.title: Capability matrix
docs.text:
S = supported within stated scope; V = unverified, U = unsupported. Required V/U refuses. Entries describe shipped adapters with the ordinary subprocess backend, no unrestricted request hooks, and characterized CLI protocol versions.

Requirement OpenAI API Anthropic API Claude Code Codex Granted host-tool protocol and shared policy S S S S Native tools unavailable S S V U Complete MCP allowlist boundary V V V V Structured answer protocol and canonical validation S S S S Usage reporting with incomplete measurement distinguished S S S S Observed spending threshold between turns S S U U Exact hard dollar cap U U U U Filesystem/network/process/credential/configuration isolation U U U U Complete descendant/provider cancellation requirement V V U U

The three Claude Code protocol rows — granted host-tool protocol, structured answer protocol, usage reporting — read S only on a binary at or above MINIMUM_TESTED_CLI_VERSION. Below it they are V and the mode refuses; strictly above it they are S with cli_protocol_version_above_tested_floor, which says the credit was inferred from a floor rather than measured on that binary. Measured on 2.1.302 under a DENY ceiling, the surviving refusals are native_tools_unavailable (V) and mcp_allowlist (V); the protocol rows no longer contribute to that refusal, which is the whole point of re-measuring them.

The API wire declares granted functions only, not provider-side MCP servers or native tools. The broader MCP_ALLOWLIST requirement also covers host MCP implementations; arbitrary host callbacks remain trusted and unverified under that broader boundary. Unrestricted request hooks make native absence and catalog/schema support unverified. The tested CLI host protocol can execute under deliberately selected non-strict policies; that does not satisfy DENY. This work never translates DENY into another policy.

docs.title: Real CLI evidence and remaining blockers
docs.text:
The real-process tests use empty temporary homes, synthetic credentials and local scripted provider endpoints. They are independent of paid/authenticated provider tests. Both providers run granted host effects, refuse denied and unattended host calls, retain actual IDs and return typed answers.

Claude Code 2.1.300 passes twelve adapter profiles: fresh/resume/fork/correction with API-key, staged-home API-key and fake OAuth-shaped saved-session credentials. The local server verifies expected authentication selection without logging the header. Planted native Read/Bash, user/project hooks and discovered MCP commands cause no effects. Skill/project-instruction canaries do not reach the provider.

docs.title: Claude Code 2.1.302, characterized
docs.text:
2.1.302 passes fifteen adapter profiles — fresh/resume/fork/correction/cancellation across the same three credential profiles — plus a schema-presence pair and a credential-separation case. The authentication profiles are load-bearing rather than decorative: the adapter drops --bare whenever a credential is staged into the home or a bearer token is used, so staged_api_key and saved_session exercise the profile that must hold WITHOUT the one flag that disables discovery wholesale. Measured directly: --bare is not load-bearing for any surface below. --setting-sources "", --tools "", --strict-mcp-config with an empty --mcp-config, and --disable-slash-commands produce an identical empty wire catalogue with and without it.

Every plant is proved CAPABLE before its exclusion is allowed to mean anything. A control run of the same binary over the same planted tree, in the same HOME/CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR layout the adapter produces, with the restriction flags removed, must fire every sentinel and put every canary on the wire. Eight sentinel files and five instruction canaries, from nine distinct surfaces:

planted surface live without restrictions executed under the adapter profile project .claude/settings.json hook yes no project .claude/settings.local.json hook yes no project .mcp.json undeclared MCP server yes no user settings.json hook (config dir) yes no plugin auto-loaded from the skills directory (hook + MCP + skill) yes no plugin installed by claude plugin marketplace add / install (hook + MCP + skill) yes no project CLAUDE.md reaches wire no user CLAUDE.md memory (config dir) reaches wire no project .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md reaches wire no

Provider-side planted tool_use for Read, MemoryRead, Bash, Write, Skill and an undeclared mcp__planted-project__* name are refused by the binary itself with No such tool available, and their sentinel files — a Bash touch and a Write outside the job directory — do not appear. The granted host operation executes in the same assistant message, so the run cannot pass by never getting far enough to attempt the violations.

Three surfaces were planted and could NOT be made to fire even with every restriction lifted, so they are recorded here and asserted on nowhere: the top-level mcpServers table in ~/.claude.json, AGENTS.md, and a CLAUDE.md inside an --add-dir directory. An unproven plant is not evidence; asserting on one manufactures a pass. Enterprise managed settings at an OS path were NOT planted — writing one needs root, and no flag agentkit passes overrides it.

Credential separation is measured as a twin rather than an absence. The local provider refuses to answer unless it receives the exact staged bearer token, so a green authentication check is positive evidence the CLI child held the credential; the same secret, the API key and the refresh token are then absent from /usr/bin/env run inside a granted host tool, and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN are absent from that subprocess entirely. No credential value appears in any argv the adapter builds. This is environment and argv separation only; the staged home is a same-user directory and a same-user process that can read it is outside this boundary.

docs.title: StructuredOutput is a protocol helper, not an authority
docs.text:
Decided explicitly, with the measurement behind it. Under the strictest profile agentkit ships, the wire catalogue is {mcp__agentkit__allowed, StructuredOutput} when a schema is requested and {mcp__agentkit__allowed} when none is — so the helper is a consequence of asking for a schema, not a resident. It carries no path, command or destination; its arguments ARE the answer and still pass the host's canonical validation and correction loop; and it produces no host invocation, hence no permission decision and no lifecycle event (the only lifecycle name observed in a schema run is the granted tool). It therefore expands no authority and needs no grant.

It is nevertheless a NATIVE tool, injected by the binary and never granted by the host, present on the wire under that same strictest profile. That is a measured counterexample to "no native tool is available", and it is now the stated reason native_tools_unavailable stays V for Claude rather than a footnote. The two facts are not in tension: the helper is safe AND native-tool absence is unproven.

Native-tool absence stays V for a second, independent reason. --tools "" and --setting-sources "" are CLI configuration, not an OS boundary: the process retains full user authority, agentkit cannot verify the binary honours a flag beyond the cases measured here, and the three plants that would not fire show the surface enumeration is demonstrably incomplete. Absence cannot be established by enumeration.

Per the owner's direction, absence is no longer the target for CLI modes. Containment — no authority beyond the admitted job — is, and it is a distinct capability: SDK modes may satisfy absence while CLI modes satisfy containment. The evidence above is containment evidence for the CONFIGURATION boundary specifically, and it is not yet sufficient for it. CONFIGURATION stays U pending: enterprise managed settings at an OS path that no agentkit flag overrides, a mechanism that makes the exclusion set enumerable rather than sampled, and environment-variable configuration surfaces. The remaining boundaries — filesystem roots including symlinks, egress filtering, process and peer separation, complete descendant reaping — are unchanged.

Tests still do not prove vendor acceptance of saved credentials or real token refresh. No paid provider turn was run for this characterization: the provider is a local socket and every credential is a synthetic string.

Codex 0.162.1 clean/planted twins use the real adapter. view_image executes and sends an outside synthetic image to the local provider under current feature restrictions and read-only sandboxing. Existing probes independently show write denial alongside allowed outside reads. This proves why DENY remains U. A complete immutable native-tools-off mechanism, including resumed sessions, is required upstream. Approval settings and read-only sandboxes cannot replace it.

Both CLIs need independently verified control-plane/tool-executor credential separation before contained native execution can be supported. The backend must then establish file roots including symlinks, egress/private-endpoint filtering, configuration discovery exclusion, process/peer separation and complete descendant reaping. A same-user temporary HOME or container sharing native tools and its auth file is insufficient. The subprocess backend establishes a private environment and process group only. Detached descendants can escape that group; cleanup cannot claim complete termination. File removal is not secure erasure. Existing credential rotation callbacks and staged credential cleanup remain.

Official mechanism references (not attestations of these binaries): Claude CLI reference, Codex configuration reference. Their current content cannot certify older binaries. Actual local tests determine the claims above.

docs.title: Standalone integration and migration
docs.text:
See tests/examples/plugin_execution/README.md and tests/examples/README.md in the repository for exact setup/run commands, the independent plugin contributions and test classifications. Cited as repository paths rather than links because those files live outside the documentation tree, and mkdocs --strict fails a link it cannot resolve to a documentation page. Only the binding changes across modes; no application-specific dispatcher or MCP service exists.

Consumers should:

  1. Build an explicitly granted ToolRegistry and attach resource permissions and observers through ToolSet. Scope must come from host context, not model args.
  2. Treat ASK as refused unless an explicit bounded host approval handler exists. Use observer return values for nothing; use permissions for policy decisions.
  3. Pass the phase's ExecutionRequirements through the existing runtime/runner. Assess before selecting a connection, then handle typed local incompatibility.
  4. Persist complete session restrictions. Older sessions reconstructed from IDs require the host to re-supply and reassess their policy ceiling.
  5. Distinguish runtime attempts, CLI internal requests, usage completeness, unpriced cost, observed thresholds and unsupported hard caps.

The consuming application retains plugin composition, tenancy, binding selection, workflow and ledger ownership. No changes to its model-call runtime are required. No package version bump or published release is included.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The final implementation passes the repository gate. Skipped or unrun checks are not enforcement evidence; protected CLI acceptance remains unmet as described above. No native-tool policy, spending limit, test assertion or coverage threshold was relaxed to make a mode execute.

docs.title: Re-verification against Claude Code 2.1.302
docs.text:
Check Result claude --version / codex --version, empty temporary home 2.1.302 (Claude Code); codex-cli 0.162.1, which self-upgraded to 0.163.0 during the session test_claude_execution_profile.py (new) 54 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed Full suite, real CLIs enabled, three consecutive randomized runs 2,837 passed, 16 skipped, 0 failed uv run ruff check agentkit tests Passed uv run mypy --strict agentkit Passed; 149 source files uv run python .github/scripts/mutants.py --verify All anchors resolve; nothing left mutated Paid provider turns none; $0 spent

Moving to a floor invalidated one existing conformance test by design rather than by regression. test_cli_version_changes_are_not_hidden_by_cache represented "an untested version" with 999.0.0, which a floor credits by construction, and asserted 2.1.300 compatible, which a 2.1.302 floor refuses. Its real invariant — a version change is not hidden by a cache — survives in planted.binary_version, so the test was re-aimed rather than deleted: the sentinel for "not characterized" is now an OLD version (0.0.1), because under a floor every future-looking sentinel is a credited one. Three further conformance tests were added alongside it so that each direction of the floor is independently pinned: at/above/below the floor per mode, below-the-floor values whose TEXT sorts above it (2.1.9, 2.1.99), and six unreadable version strings that must refuse.

Observed red before the code changed, in order: the new file's import of the version table (symbol absent); then, once the gate was made isinstance-based, all twelve existing real-adapter Claude profiles refused with cli_protocol_version_unverified on 2.1.302 — the finding that the gate had been inert for subclassed backends; then the new characterization's fifteen profiles refused the same way with zero processes started, which is the failure the pin entry had to earn. The entry was added as a hypothesis and the characterization confirmed it; had it failed, the entry comes back out.

Two fixture bugs were found and are worth recording because each produced a green-looking wrong answer. Annotating a host tool's ctx parameter pulled it into the generated JSON Schema, so every granted call came back Tool arguments do not match the granted schema while the run still answered through the schema helper — an "effect never happened" that looks like a passing test unless the effect itself is asserted. And a content_block_start carrying the final text with no following text_delta is accepted by a lenient parser and ignored by the real client: 2.1.302 accumulated an empty assistant message, kept looping and returned result: "", which surfaces as transport produced no answer.

Not run, and therefore not claimed: no paid model turn was made against either CLI or either API for this work, so nothing here attests vendor acceptance of the saved-session credential shape, vendor token refresh, or the behaviour of a real model choosing to call a granted tool on 2.1.302. The opt-in command for that step is set -a && source .env.eval && set +a && AGENTKIT_LIVE=1 uv run pytest tests/source/live -q -p no:randomly, on claude-haiku-4-5 / gpt-4o-mini; it is a handful of short turns, on the order of a few cents, and it remains unfunded and unrun.

Mutation entries for the new gate are warranted and were NOT added, because .github/scripts/mutants.py is out of scope for this change. Four mutants would each be killed by a named new test:

  • comparing version strings instead of parsed release numbers → test_the_floor_compares_release_numbers_and_never_version_text
  • treating an unparseable version as passing the floor → test_a_version_string_that_cannot_be_read_never_passes_the_floor
  • turning not _at_least(...) into a strict > (off-by-one at the floor) → test_a_binary_below_the_tested_floor_refuses_the_protocol_profile
  • restoring type(...) is SubprocessExecutionBackend → test_a_backend_subclass_cannot_dodge_the_version_gate

Focused regressions were observed red before behavior changes: 14 host-policy cases, 14 real-adapter CLI identity/context cases, four adapter receipt cases, four asynchronous configuration-mutation cases, two missing-usage cases (their two measured-zero twins already passed), the protected backend-port case, and three implicit-DENY cases (Codex already refused). All four example-layout tests failed on the former flat layout before the moves. Tests also caught private exception leakage before adding the explicit safe-error contract. Fixture errors were corrected separately and are not enforcement evidence.

Intermediate broad gates reported 20 failed/2,648 passed/55 skipped, then three failed/2,666 passed/55 skipped. They exposed recovery messages being hidden and a forwarding test relying on an unassessed adapter under DENY. Curated business and framework recovery messages now use explicit safe failures; their effect, approval, idempotency and accounting assertions remain. The forwarding fixture now identifies its no-process scripted transport explicitly, and a separate four-mode guard test requires zero dispatch from an unassessed adapter. An intermediate mutation baseline reported two gateway failures and correctly stopped without claiming mutation success; the final baseline and catalogue pass.

The mutation runner used --allow-dirty only inside a disposable copy with its own virtual environment. No source mutation ran in the working repository or overlapped tests against its source. Five new mutants cover host DENY, unattended approval, input validation, stale receipts and transport body bounds. An existing backend-guarantee mutant was re-anchored to the stronger refusal condition.
